source.title: Implicit Gradient Alignment in Distributed and Federated Learning
source.authors: Yatin Dandi; Luis Barba; Martin Jaggi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: Compares an adapted large-batch training method with large-batch SGD and reports test accuracy, using a different intervention from the original large-batch studies.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports federated test-accuracy comparisons and gradient-variance measurements. Those settings do not test the fixed-epoch large-batch claim or the specific sharpness measure in V7. Cited results from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study uses the large-batch generalization finding to motivate GradAlign and reports its method's performance against other optimizers. It does not compare small and large batches under a controlled fixed epoch budget or establish that the large-batch penalty is removed. Its gradient-alignment results do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' interpretation: GradAlign is designed to reproduce SGD's implicit gradient alignment with large batches, and it outperforms large-batch SGD on CIFAR-10 by test accuracy and update count. The authors also report federated image-classification improvements. Retention of small-batch generalization is their interpretation, rather than a demonstrated match to a controlled small-batch baseline; they acknowledge tuning and computational overhead.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes gradient-alignment displacement to adapt large-batch training; the comparison is organized by number of updates rather than the fixed-epoch setup in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that batch size affects FedGA and SCAFFOLD more than FedAvg in heterogeneous federated learning; these comparisons do not test V5's fixed-epoch condition. It also reports that FedGA's benefit depends on tuning β and that its advantage was absent on the Shakespeare next-character task.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10, GradAlign achieves higher test accuracy than large-batch SGD and converges faster by parameter-update count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-alignment displacement can improve large-batch optimizer performance in the tested CNN setting.

fits_no_version.finding: FedGA improves test performance in several image-classification settings and reduces measured inter-client gradient differences; it provides no advantage over FedAvg on Shakespeare, where those differences are already small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefits of inter-client gradient alignment depend on the task and existing alignment of client gradients.

record.problems: Large-batch comparison is described qualitatively in text and its values are figure-only; the paper does not hold epoch budget fixed for that comparison. Experiments use a simple CNN and the authors note omitted practical hyperparameters and Taylor-approximation limitations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for federated method comparisons or gradient-variance plots: those are not large-batch fixed-epoch outcomes or V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure. The text reports these elsewhere in Sections 5.1–5.2 and Figures 2, 5, 7, 9, and 10.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

The large-versus-small-batch held-out penalty under fixed epoch budgets, its workload-dependent threshold, and its removal relative to a measured small-batch baseline. Batch sizes and local steps are tuned, and comparisons emphasize updates, communication rounds, or maximum accuracy.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the V5 limits_scope verdict: an uncontrolled epoch budget is an untested condition, not evidence limiting the claim. The paper also inconsistently describes the CIFAR-10 CNN as having two fully connected layers in Section 5.2 and three in Appendix B.1. No additional eligible version-specific results are missing from the record.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
The paper compares methods by number of updates, not a controlled fixed-epoch budget. It does not map workload-dependent batch thresholds across image and language tasks.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: Large-Batch SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared with GradAlign on CIFAR10 in the setting minimizing number of updates.
rows.locator: Figure 2, bottom; Section 5.2, “Minimizing number of updates”
rows.note: The text says GradAlign achieves noticeably higher test accuracy than Large-Batch SGD, but the precise plotted value is not stated.
rows.check: This is a comparator in a method-performance comparison, not a measured large-versus-small-batch penalty under fixed epochs. The batch sizes 1000 and 5000 are per worker; with ten participating workers, the aggregate sizes are 10000 and 50000. They are tuning candidates, not separately identified plotted conditions.

rows.subject: GradAlign
rows.operation_detail: Uses gradient alignment with large mini-batches; compared with Large-Batch SGD and SCAFFOLD (large-batch).
rows.locator: Figure 2, bottom; Section 5.2, “Minimizing number of updates”
rows.note: Authors state GradAlign noticeably achieves higher test accuracy than Large-Batch SGD and converges faster in number of updates.
rows.check: Higher accuracy than large-batch SGD establishes a method improvement, not recovery of a measured small-batch baseline under the same epoch budget. The observed state cannot be assigned to V5. Batch sizes are per-worker tuning candidates, and GradAlign also computes gradients for the displacement.

rows.subject: SCAFFOLD (LargeBatch)
rows.operation_detail: Compared with GradAlign and Large-Batch SGD on CIFAR10 in the setting minimizing number of updates.
rows.locator: Figure 2, bottom; Section 5.2, “Minimizing number of updates”
rows.note: The text states the comparison shows GradAlign achieves noticeably higher test accuracy than Large-Batch SGD; it gives no explicit comparison with large-batch SCAFFOLD.
rows.check: This is another method comparator without the small-batch baseline and fixed epoch comparison V5 requires. The text does not specify its numerical accuracy. Batch sizes are per-worker tuning candidates rather than separately reported outcomes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
